options: SELECT u.name, l.rating FROM Users u JOIN Listens l ON u.user_id = l.user_id WHERE l.rating IS NOT NULL
SELECT u.name, l.rating FROM Users u JOIN Listens l ON u.user_id = l.user_id
SELECT u.name, l.rating FROM Users u LEFT JOIN Listens l ON u.user_id = l.user_id
SELECT u.name, l.rating FROM Users u LEFT JOIN Listens l ON u.user_id = l.user_id WHERE l.rating IS NULL
m1.explanation:
The difference to look for: a WHERE on the right table's column drops the NULL-extended padding rows, so the LEFT JOIN collapses to an inner join.

So the keyed query (an inner join with the same filter) returns identical rows. Each wrong option drops or flips the filter: the bare inner join still includes Daffy's real listen whose rating is NULL, the bare LEFT JOIN additionally keeps Pluto's padded NULL row, and the IS NULL version returns the opposite rows.

m1.question:
The reference tags each listen with its user's highest rating (a window/ladder). Which query is query-equivalent?
Reference query:
SELECT listen_id, MAX(rating) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id) AS m
FROM Listens
options: SELECT listen_id, MAX(rating) OVER () AS m FROM Listens
SELECT listen_id, AVG(rating) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id) AS m FROM Listens
SELECT l.listen_id, (SELECT MAX(rating) FROM Listens l2 WHERE l2.user_id = l.user_id) AS m FROM Listens l
SELECT l.listen_id, (SELECT MAX(rating) FROM Listens) AS m FROM Listens l
m1.explanation:
The difference to look for: a partitioned window MAX equals a correlated MAX over the same partition.

Both keep every listen row; only the per-user maximum has to match, and the correlated subquery's WHERE l2.user_id = l.user_id reproduces the window's partition. Each wrong option changes exactly one piece: OVER () drops the partition and gives the global max, AVG changes the aggregate, and the uncorrelated subquery removes the per-user filter so every row shows the same global max.

m1.question:
Consider these two queries:
-- Query A: GROUP BY
SELECT user_id, song_id,
       ROUND(CAST(AVG(rating) AS NUMERIC), 2) as avg_rating
FROM Listens
GROUP BY user_id, song_id
ORDER BY user_id, song_id;
-- Query B: WINDOW
SELECT user_id, song_id, rating,
       ROUND(CAST(AVG(rating) OVER
         (PARTITION BY user_id) AS NUMERIC), 2) as user_avg
FROM Listens
ORDER BY user_id, song_id;
What is the key difference between GROUP BY and window functions?
options: GROUP BY collapses rows into one per group; window functions keep every row and add a column
Window functions collapse rows into one per partition, exactly as GROUP BY does per group
GROUP BY supports only COUNT; window functions are the only way to apply AVG or SUM
There is no real difference; the two queries always return identical rows and columns
m1.explanation: GROUP BY collapses multiple rows into one row per group. Window functions (OVER + PARTITION BY) keep all original rows and add a computed aggregate as a new column. Each row retains its individual rating while also showing the user-level average.

m1.question: The section wraps the model's generation in three steps, each catching a different failure. Match precision, execution, and verification to the failure each one catches.
options: Precision catches crashes; execution catches the wrong reading; verification catches drift
Precision catches the wrong reading; execution catches crashes and empty results; verification catches subtle errors and drift
Precision catches drift; execution catches the wrong reading; verification catches crashes
All three catch the same failure, a wrong answer, at different points in the pipeline
m1.explanation: Precision (the spec) catches a query that runs but answers the wrong reading. Execution (running on real data) catches crashes and empty results. Verification (testing the result and re-running the test) catches subtle errors and definitions that drift over time.

m1.question: A model is wired to a database so it can run its query, read the error, and retry (multi-shot) instead of emitting one blind query (one-shot). Multi-shot raises accuracy, but it still tops out well below correct. Why?
options: Retrying fixes a query that crashes or returns nothing, but it cannot fix a query that runs and answers the wrong question
Each retry costs tokens, so the model gives up before it finds the right query
Multi-shot only helps on simple queries; complex joins still fail to compile
The database returns rows in a different order each run, so the model never converges
m1.explanation: Running and retrying catches mechanical failures (a crash, an empty result) for free. It cannot catch a query that runs cleanly and means the wrong thing, because the database has no opinion about your intent. Closing that gap needs precision (the spec) and verification.

m1.question: A unit test and a regression test are the same check used two ways. What is the difference?
options: A unit test checks one query; a regression test checks the whole database schema at once
A unit test asks whether the query is right now; a regression test re-runs that check on every change, so you learn the day a definition stops being right
A unit test is written in SQL; a regression test is written in Python
A unit test is run by hand; a regression test is a different test you author from scratch
m1.explanation: The difference is time. A unit test answers "is this query right?" once. Keep it and re-run it on every change and it answers "is it still right?". The day a definition silently shifts, the stored test fails that day, not months later.

m1.question: The section argues that multishot, verification, and composition all depend on SQL specifically, not English. What property of SQL makes that work?
options: SQL is the most popular query language, so models are trained on more of it
SQL is exact, and you can run it, test its output, and build on it; you can do none of that to an English sentence
SQL queries are shorter than English descriptions, so they are easier to read
SQL hides the data model, so the model needs less context
m1.explanation: The retry loop, the test, and the library all need something you can run, re-run, and compose. SQL is that artifact: exact and executable. You cannot run an English sentence, re-run it after a change, or build a bigger query on top of it. That is why SQL is the spine.

m1.question: Claude answers Anthropic's internal business questions at 21% bare and 95% wrapped in the stack. Giving the model the company's entire history of past SQL queries, raw, moved accuracy less than one point. What does that say about the 21 to 95 jump?
options: It came from a larger, smarter model trained on the company's data
It came from structure (a governed semantic layer and skills that route the model to the right definitions), not from raw access to more SQL
It came mostly from letting the model retry more times (multi-shot)
It came from giving the model read access to every table in the warehouse
m1.explanation: Same model in both runs, so it is not a smarter model. Raw access to all past SQL moved accuracy less than a point, so access is not the bottleneck. The lift came from precision built as infrastructure: a semantic layer that pins definitions and skills that route the model to the docs that matter. Structure does the work, not access.

m2.question: Why does keeping related data physically close on disk speed up access?
options: The disk physically spins faster when the data is clustered together
Clustered data needs no index at all to be looked up efficiently
Locality matters only inside RAM and has no effect on disk access
Nearby rows ride in one page or run, so a single IO serves many of them
m2.explanation: Spatial locality lets one page read (or one sequential run) satisfy many row accesses, cutting total IOs. Clustering and good layout exploit this.

m2.question: Why does the system read and write whole pages instead of individual rows?
options: Pages compress far better than individual rows, which saves disk space
Individual rows simply cannot be addressed or located from within SQL
The device transfers a fixed block per access, so the page is the unit of IO
Reading whole pages is what prevents two keys from hashing together
m2.explanation: Storage is block-addressed: the device moves a fixed-size page per access. The page is therefore the IO unit, and the cost model counts pages, not rows.

m2.question: Order these by access latency, fastest first:
options: network round trip < spinning disk < SSD < RAM
RAM < SSD < spinning disk < network round trip
SSD < RAM < network round trip < spinning disk
spinning disk < RAM < SSD < network round trip
m2.explanation: Each level down the hierarchy is orders of magnitude slower: RAM (ns) < SSD (µs) < disk (ms) < network (10s of ms). The gaps are why the IO cost model treats a page read as expensive.

m2.question: What does the buffer pool (page cache) do?
options: Permanently holds the whole database so the disk becomes unnecessary
Keeps recently used pages in RAM so repeat accesses skip the disk read
Compresses each page in memory to cut the space it takes on disk
Reorders pending writes so they reach the disk in sequential order
m2.explanation: The buffer pool caches hot pages in memory; a hit avoids a disk IO entirely. Hit rate is why working-set size and eviction policy matter.

m2.question: What is the trade-off in choosing a larger page size?
options: Larger pages are simply faster for every workload across the board
Larger pages hold so much data they remove the need for an index
Large pages cut per-IO overhead for scans but waste them on a point lookup
Page size has no real effect on the IO cost of any query at all
m2.explanation: Bigger pages mean fewer IOs for big sequential scans, but a point lookup still drags a whole page, wasting transfer and buffer space. The right size depends on the access pattern.

m2.question: Why does a random-read workload favor an SSD over a spinning disk far more than a sequential one does?
options: An SSD simply stores far more total data than a spinning disk can
Sequential reads actually run slower on an SSD than on a spinning disk
A spinning disk pays no seek cost whatsoever when it does a random read
A disk seeks per random read; an SSD has no seek, so random nears sequential
m2.explanation: Random access on a disk pays a seek (head movement) per read; an SSD has no seek, so random reads stay near sequential speed. The gap is largest for random workloads.

m2.question: Why does compressing a table often speed up a scan, even with decompression cost?
options: Compression removes the need to scan the table at all on most queries
Fewer bytes means fewer page reads, and the saved IO outweighs decompress CPU
Decompression runs for free on modern CPUs, so it adds no cost ever
Compressed pages skip the buffer pool, saving a layer of memory copies
m2.explanation: Compression shrinks page count, and on big data IO dominates. Reading fewer pages and paying cheap CPU to decompress is usually a net win.

m2.scenario_stem: Table R has P(R) = 1,000 pages. Cost is modeled as Cr·(pages read) + Cw·(pages written); CPU is ignored. Assume Cr = Cw = c.
m2.question: Algorithm A1 reads every page once and writes every page once. Total cost?
m2.explanation: Cost = C<sub>r</sub>·P + C<sub>w</sub>·P = c·1,000 + c·1,000 = 2,000c.

m2.scenario_stem: Table R has P(R) = 1,000 pages. Cost is modeled as Cr·(pages read) + Cw·(pages written); CPU is ignored. Assume Cr = Cw = c.
m2.question: Algorithm A2 reads all pages 3 times and writes all pages once. Total cost?
m2.explanation: Cost = C<sub>r</sub>·3P + C<sub>w</sub>·1P = c·3,000 + c·1,000 = 4,000c. Each extra pass over the data adds P more IOs.

m2.scenario_stem: Table R has P(R) = 1,000 pages. Cost is modeled as Cr·(pages read) + Cw·(pages written); CPU is ignored. Assume Cr = Cw = c.
m2.question: Algorithm A1 costs 5·P IOs; algorithm A2 costs P·log₂P IOs. At P = 1,000, which is cheaper?
options: A2 at 9,966c, since a log factor always beats a constant factor
They tie at 5,000c, since both costs are simply linear in P
A1 at 5,000c, since 5·P < P·log₂P ≈ 9,966 at this P = 1,000
Cannot tell, since the answer needs C<sub>r</sub> and C<sub>w</sub> split out
m2.explanation: 5·P = 5,000; P·log₂P = 1,000·10.0 ≈ 9,966. The constant-factor linear scan wins at this size. Asymptotics can mislead when the data is only a few thousand pages.

m2.scenario_stem: Table R has P(R) = 1,000 pages. Cost is modeled as Cr·(pages read) + Cw·(pages written); CPU is ignored. Assume Cr = Cw = c.
m2.question: Why does the model count only page reads/writes and ignore CPU work?
options: CPUs are simply too slow to matter once the data gets large
The model assumes the whole table already fits in RAM
Writes hit disk for free, so only page reads are counted
A page IO costs ~10<sup>6</sup> times a CPU compare, so IO dominates runtime
m2.explanation: On data larger than RAM, moving a page dwarfs a CPU comparison by ~10^6. Saving one IO is worth ~10 million CPU ops, so total runtime tracks IO count.

m2.scenario_stem: Table R has P(R) = 1,000 pages. Cost is modeled as Cr·(pages read) + Cw·(pages written); CPU is ignored. Assume Cr = Cw = c.
m2.question: Reading the same P(R) pages sequentially vs in random order: how do the costs compare?
options: Sequential streams contiguous pages; random seeks per page, so it costs more
They cost the same, since an IO is an IO no matter the page order taken
Random is faster, since it gets to skip the pages the query never needs
Order only matters for writes; reads end up costing the same either way
m2.explanation: C_r hides an access (seek) plus transfer term. Sequential access amortizes the seek across a contiguous run; random access pays a seek per page. Same page count, very different real cost, which is why layout and clustering matter.

m2.question: Why does a column store usually compress better than a row store?
options: A single column simply contains fewer rows than the full table
A column holds one low-variety type, so runs and dictionaries pack it tight
A row store cannot be compressed at all, only a column store
Compression works only on numeric columns, never on text ones
m2.explanation: Storing one column together groups similar, low-cardinality values, which run-length and dictionary encoding squeeze hard. Mixed-type rows compress far less, which is one reason OLAP uses columnar layout.

m2.question: Why does fragmentation hurt a large sequential scan?
options: It shrinks the total usable capacity of the disk the table sits on
It quietly corrupts the actual data stored on the fragmented pages
Adjacent pages scatter on disk, turning cheap sequential reads into random ones
It slows writes only; a read scan is never affected by fragmentation
m2.explanation: Fragmentation breaks physical contiguity, so a scan that should stream contiguous pages instead seeks between scattered ones, paying random-IO cost.

m2.question: What is write amplification?
options: The disk writes more physical bytes than the app logically wrote to it
Writing the very same record out to several replicas for durability
Compressing each write so that fewer total bytes ever hit the disk
Buffering many writes together in memory before flushing them once
m2.explanation: Write amplification is the ratio of physical bytes written to logical bytes written. Block-granular media and log-structured merges both inflate it, which matters for SSD wear and throughput.

m2.scenario_stem: A hash table with B = 10 buckets uses h(x) = x mod 10. Insert keys: 42, 157, 1042, 89, 22, 60.
m2.question: Which bucket does key 1042 land in?
m2.explanation: h(1042) = 1042 mod 10 = 2. Modulo hashing keys on the last digit here, so 1042 shares a bucket with 42 and 22.

m2.scenario_stem: A hash table with B = 10 buckets uses h(x) = x mod 10. Insert keys: 42, 157, 1042, 89, 22, 60.
m2.question: Which keys collide (land in the same bucket)?
options: 157 and 89 (both are odd, so they share a bucket)
60 and 89 (consecutive buckets count as a collision)
22, 42, and 1042 (each ends in 2, so bucket 2)
None: distinct keys always land in distinct buckets
m2.explanation: h(x)=x mod 10 keys on the last digit: 22, 42, 1042 all end in 2 → bucket 2. The table needs chaining or open addressing there.

m2.scenario_stem: A hash table with B = 10 buckets uses h(x) = x mod 10. Insert keys: 42, 157, 1042, 89, 22, 60.
m2.question: Bucket 2 now holds several keys. What is the difference between chaining and open addressing?
options: Chaining doubles the table on a collision; open addressing never resizes it
They are two names for the same technique, differing only in wording
Open addressing can lose keys to false negatives; chaining cannot lose any
Chaining hangs a list off the bucket; open addressing probes for the next free slot
m2.explanation: Chaining hangs a list off the colliding bucket; open addressing places the key in the next free slot by a probe sequence. Both resolve collisions; they trade memory for probe cost.

m2.scenario_stem: A hash table with B = 10 buckets uses h(x) = x mod 10. Insert keys: 42, 157, 1042, 89, 22, 60.
m2.question: Using a hash index on this key, how many IOs does an equality lookup cost (vs a full scan)?
options: 1 IO: hash straight to the bucket's page and read just it
P(R) IOs: hashing still has to scan every page to find the key
log P(R) IOs: a hash lookup descends levels like a B+tree does
0 IOs: the hash returns the row from the key without any read
m2.explanation: Hashing drives equality lookup to expected 1 IO: compute the bucket, read its page. A full scan costs P(R) IOs. That 1-vs-P(R) gap is the whole point of a hash index.

m2.scenario_stem: A hash table with B = 10 buckets uses h(x) = x mod 10. Insert keys: 42, 157, 1042, 89, 22, 60.
m2.question: Why can a hash table's O(1) lookup degrade in practice?
options: Modulo hashing is collision-free, so lookups can never slow down at all
A weak hash or skewed keys pile into a few buckets, so lookups drift toward O(n)
Collisions make the hash start returning false negatives on present keys
Buckets auto-rebalance to stay uniform, so O(1) holds for any key set
m2.explanation: Expected O(1) assumes a uniform spread. A weak hash or skewed keys overload a few buckets; those chains grow and lookups approach O(n). A good hash and load-factor headroom keep it near 1 IO.

m2.question: What happens as a hash table's load factor (keys per bucket) climbs too high?
options: Lookups speed up, since the denser table packs keys closer together
The hash function swaps itself out automatically for a wider one
Collisions become impossible once every bucket holds at least one key
Chains grow with collisions, so lookups slow toward O(n) until a resize
m2.explanation: A high load factor means many keys per bucket, so collision chains lengthen and the expected O(1) lookup degrades. Resizing (rehashing into more buckets) restores it.

m2.question: A hash index gives 1-IO equality lookups. Why might you still pick a B+tree?
options: A B+tree always beats a hash index on IO count for equality lookups
A hash index simply cannot store or look up duplicate key values
A hash index can't do range or ordered scans; a B+tree does both plus equality
A B+tree answers every query from memory, needing no disk reads
m2.explanation: Hashing destroys key order, so range and ORDER BY queries fall back to a scan. A B+tree keeps keys sorted and linked, answering equality, range, and ordered access.

m2.question: How does locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) differ from a normal hash?
options: LSH makes similar items collide on purpose, enabling nearest-neighbor search
LSH guarantees zero collisions, spreading every item to its own bucket
LSH is reversible: you can decode the bucket back to the original input
LSH applies only to integer keys, not to vectors or text or images
m2.explanation: A normal hash scatters similar inputs to spread load. LSH does the opposite: near points hash to the same bucket with high probability, so you scan one bucket to find approximate neighbors.

m2.scenario_stem: A Bloom filter uses m = 9,600,000 bits for n = 1,000,000 keys, with k hash functions. Recall p = (1 − e−kn/m)k and k* = (m/n)·ln 2.
m2.question: Which number of hash functions k minimizes the false-positive rate?
m2.explanation: k* = (m/n)·ln 2 = (9,600,000/1,000,000)·0.693 = 6.65, so k = 7. Too few or too many hashes both raise the false-positive rate.

m2.scenario_stem: A Bloom filter uses m = 9,600,000 bits for n = 1,000,000 keys, with k hash functions. Recall p = (1 − e−kn/m)k and k* = (m/n)·ln 2.
m2.question: Using the optimal k = 7, the false-positive rate is closest to:
m2.explanation: p = (1 − e<sup>−7·1,000,000/9,600,000</sup>)<sup>7</sup> ≈ 0.0100 ≈ 1%. That is the ~1% rate the page cites for ~10 bits/item at k ≈ 7.

m2.scenario_stem: A Bloom filter uses m = 9,600,000 bits for n = 1,000,000 keys, with k hash functions. Recall p = (1 − e−kn/m)k and k* = (m/n)·ln 2.
m2.question: About how many bits per key does this filter use?
options: 1 bits
7 bits
9 bits
18 bits
m2.explanation: m/n = 9,600,000/1,000,000 = 9.6 bits per key, the ~10 bits/item the page cites. That small budget is why a billion-key filter fits in ~1.25 GB.

m2.scenario_stem: A Bloom filter uses m = 9,600,000 bits for n = 1,000,000 keys, with k hash functions. Recall p = (1 − e−kn/m)k and k* = (m/n)·ln 2.
m2.question: Can a lookup wrongly report a key is NOT in the set (a false negative)?
options: No: an inserted key's k bits stay 1, so 'not in set' is always correct
Yes: a set bit can be cleared, dropping a key that was inserted
Yes: once the filter is over half full, inserted keys go missing
Yes: when two keys share bits, one of them reads as absent
m2.explanation: Every inserted key set its k bits to 1, so they stay 1; a 0 bit proves absence. False positives are possible, false negatives are not.

m2.scenario_stem: A Bloom filter uses m = 9,600,000 bits for n = 1,000,000 keys, with k hash functions. Recall p = (1 − e−kn/m)k and k* = (m/n)·ln 2.
m2.question: If we keep m and k fixed but insert many more keys, what happens to accuracy?
options: The false-positive rate falls, since a fuller array rejects more lookups
The false-positive rate rises, since more set bits make collisions likelier
Nothing changes, since the rate depends only on m and never on n
False negatives appear, since crowded bits start hiding inserted keys
m2.explanation: More keys set more bits to 1 (n grows in (1 − e<sup>−kn/m</sup>)<sup>k</sup>), so more lookups hit all-ones by chance. The false-positive rate rises; false negatives never occur.

m2.question: Where does a Bloom filter save the most work?
options: Returning the row's actual value directly, with no page read at all
Sorting the keys up front so a following range scan runs faster
Shrinking the data on disk so each page read transfers fewer bytes
Guarding a costly lookup: a 'definitely not' skips the disk read on true misses
m2.explanation: A Bloom filter turns most true misses into a cheap in-memory 'no', skipping the page read. It never stores values, so a 'maybe' still needs the real read.

m2.question: Why can't a standard Bloom filter support deletion by clearing bits?
options: A set bit may be shared, so clearing it for one key hides the others
A Bloom filter has no bits at all to clear, only hash outputs
Clearing bits is fine but it would make every lookup much slower
Plain bit-clearing deletion works and never causes any error at all
m2.explanation: Each key sets k bits, and bits overlap across keys. Clearing a bit to delete one key can flip another key's membership to a false negative, which a Bloom filter must never produce. Counting Bloom filters address this.

m4.question: What is the fundamental rule of Two-Phase Locking (2PL)?
options: All locks must be acquired before any reads or writes
Once a lock is released, no new locks can be acquired
Locks must be released in the reverse order they were acquired
m4.explanation: 2PL has two phases: growing (acquire locks, no releases) and shrinking (release locks, no acquisitions). The first unlock marks the transition to shrinking phase.

m4.question: Under Two-Phase Locking, what marks the boundary between the growing phase and the shrinking phase?
options: The first lock the transaction releases (the first unlock)
The first lock the transaction acquires
The transaction's COMMIT record
The first write the transaction performs
m4.explanation: 2PL has a growing phase (only acquire locks) then a shrinking phase (only release). The first unlock is the transition point: after it, the transaction may never acquire another lock.

m4.question: How does Strict 2PL (S2PL) differ from regular 2PL?
options: S2PL acquires all locks at the beginning of the transaction
S2PL holds all locks until the transaction commits or aborts
S2PL only uses shared locks, not exclusive locks
m4.explanation: S2PL extends 2PL by holding all locks until commit/abort, eliminating the shrinking phase during execution. This prevents cascading aborts.

m4.question: Which single case still causes one transaction to block another under MVCC?
options: A reader and a writer touching the same row
Two transactions reading the same row
Two transactions writing the same row
m4.explanation: Two writes to the same row serialize: the second waits on a row lock until the first commits or aborts. This is the one lock MVCC keeps, and it touches only that row. Reader/writer and reader/reader pairs never block.

m4.question: What exactly is a transaction's snapshot under MVCC?
options: A full private copy of the database made when the transaction begins
A single timestamp, taken when the transaction begins, that fixes which version of each value it reads
The set of rows the transaction has locked so far
m4.explanation: A snapshot is one timestamp taken at transaction start. From then on every read returns each value as it stood at that instant: one consistent view of the whole database, with no copy.

m4.question: When several committed versions of a row exist, which one does a transaction read?
options: The newest version whose writer committed at or before the transaction's snapshot
Always the most recent version, regardless of when it was committed
The oldest version that has not yet been vacuumed
m4.explanation: The test for each read is: is this version's writer committed at or before your snapshot? Among the versions that pass, you read the newest. A version committed after your snapshot is too new to see.

m4.question: T1 is running a long read over the Listens table when T2 issues an UPDATE to one of the rows T1 will scan. Under MVCC, what happens?
options: T1 blocks until T2 commits, then reads the new value
T2 blocks until T1's read finishes
Neither blocks: T2 writes a new version, and T1 keeps reading the version visible as of its snapshot
T1 aborts with a serialization error
m4.explanation: Readers and writers never block each other in MVCC. T2 adds a new version of the row; T1 keeps reading the version current as of its snapshot. No waiting, no abort.

The scan evicts hot OLTP pages from the buffer cache
The 10-minute snapshot pins the xmin horizon and stalls VACUUM
